name: Labor market programme spending
description:
Labor market policy (LMP) database provides information on active labor market policies and social security systems explicitly targeted to people with difficulties in the labor market: the unemployed, people at risk of involuntary job loss and inactive people who would like to enter the labor market.

For more information, see Coverage and classification of the OECD data on labor market programs
Last data update: October 2023

OECD statistics contact: ELS.Contact@oecd.org

source_notes: OECD dates the United States' pandemic employment-maintenance spending to 2019, which is why the American total reads 3.37 per cent of GDP that year against 0.25 in 2018 and 0.23 in 2021. The programme it records began in April 2020, and every other country's pandemic peak falls in 2020. Read the American 2019 and 2020 figures together rather than separately.

Sub-categories do not always sum to the category above them. Across 12,974 parent and child comparisons the two agree in about seven cases in eight; where they differ the children usually fall short, because some spending sits in the broader category without being attributed to a specific programme type. In a smaller number of country-years the children exceed the parent instead, which OECD's own tables carry. Read a sub-category as a floor on what that programme type costs rather than as an exact share of its parent.

Regional rows such as OECD, EU27 and G7 are compiled from whichever member countries reported that particular figure in that particular year, so what they cover changes between one selection and the next. Two things follow. A breakdown can exceed the total it belongs to, because the two are built from different sets of countries. And a count for a region can come out far too small, because only some members reported it. Compare countries directly where the question allows it; read the regional rows as a rough centre of gravity rather than as a measurement of the region.
